newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: S.Leone student killed as army halts march - radio.
newsitem.headline: S.Leone student killed as army halts march - radio.

text.p: One student was killed and 35 people arrested on Monday when troops clashed with students protesting against army rule in Sierra Leone, state radio said.
Witnesses said the clash took place outside the Sierra Leone Nursing School in the centre of the capital Freetown where students took refuge after troops earlier cordoned off the area.
"The students tried to leave the nursing school to march when the soldiers moved in," one witness said.
State radio suggested there was an exchange of fire between the marchers and soldiers but witnesses could not confirm this.
A military spokesman told BBC Africa Service radio earlier that at least two students had been caught with AK-47 assault rifles ahead of the planned protest march.
A student union leader confirmed that a student had been wounded fatally by soldiers.
State radio also said troops broke up a similar protest march by students in the southern provincial capital Boh but gave no account of casualties or arrests.

The radio said only seven of the 35 arrested in Freetown were students, suggesting that other people had joined the first street protest against the military junta that seized power on May 25, ousting elected president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Earlier a show of force by troops prevented most students from joining the march to demand the reinstatement of Kabbah, who is exiled in neighbouring Guinea.
Hundreds of soldiers and former rebels backing the military patrolled Freetown streets in jeeps and on foot, while others searched motorists at roadblocks.
Troops brandishing rocket propelled grenades and machetes swarmed around the city's Eastend district, the planned starting point of the march by the National Union of Sierra Leone students.
Other soldiers blocked off the only road leading to Freetown's Fourah Bay College on a hill above the city.
Witnesses said then some student leaders had been arrested while several others were in hiding.
"Nothing is going to stop us," one student leader said from hiding. "We may not come out today but maybe next week."
The protests were the first serious internal challenge to junta leader Major Johnny Paul Koroma since the coup, which was led by junior officers.
Rebels who had waged a five-year guerrilla war and accused Kabbah of dishonouring a peace accord with them rallied to the coup and entered the capital in thousands.
The toppling of Kabbah, just over a year after he won elections ending four years of military rule, has been condemned by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) has imposed a land, sea and air blockade on Sierra Leone. Troops of its Nigerian-led military wing, ECOMOG, have clashed repeatedly with junta soldiers and their rebel allies.
Police banned the planned march on the grounds of security and vowed to deal ruthlessly with violations of the ban.
Tension rose sharply in the city ahead of the planned march.

The few shops that had reopened in Freetown after the pillaging that followed the coup were shut again on Monday. The Sierra Leone Commercial Bank, the only bank which obeyed orders from the military to reopen, shut its doors again on Monday.
The streets were largely emptied of traffic and pedestrians, with large crowds gathered at street corners to watch the show of force by the military.
Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha, who heads ECOWAS, visited Ivory Coast and Guinea on Monday for talks with their leaders on Sierra Leone, officials said.
Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Guinea and Ghana are members of a special committee of the 16-nation ECOWAS dealing with the Sierra Leone crisis.
Abacha is due to host a full ECOWAS summit in Abuja on August 27-29 when the Sierra Leone crisis will be a top item on the agenda, Nigerian and Ivorian officials said.
Talks between foreign ministers of the ECOWAS committee and envoys of the Freetown junta broke down last month in Abidjan after junta leader Koroma said he would retain power until 2001.
